accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core F-BF.A.2 (write arithmetic sequences explicitly and recursively), F-IF.A.3 (sequences are functions on a subset of the integers) and F-LE.A.2, plus the DfE GCSE Mathematics subject content (nth term dn + c of linear sequences, A12/A25). Every worked value was recomputed: a(10) of 5, 8, 11 is 32; 59 is term 14 of 7, 11, 15; 100 gives n = 20.4 in 3, 8, 13; a(16) = −5 is the first negative term of 100, 93, 86; the intercept a(1) − d is the zeroth term.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: the off-by-one a(1) + nd (predict a(10) = 35, item m1 Mia, challenge tag off), using the first term as the constant c (formula step options + a and tag first), sign of d in falling sequences (rounds 20, 16, 12 and 10, 7, 4, tag sign), joining points as if non-whole n has a term (Which term? 'Not a term' rounds, tag between/round) and the multiples-of-d test (m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagarith is the first lab on sequences as functions: bars that the learner builds from a(1) and d, then the same terms as points with a draggable fitted line, then the symbolic dn + c choice, then solving a(n) = value on an n track. flagline teaches y = mx + c from a taxi meter on a continuous graph, and flaggradf is calculus; neither has discrete terms, the n − 1 step count or term membership.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step moves one idea: Build makes d visible as equal bar rises and a(1) as the first bar; Points on a line makes the slope equal d and puts the intercept one step before a(1) at n = 0; Write the formula turns that into dn + c; Which term? inverts the formula; Explore shows d = 0 gives a flat line and a(1) = d gives a line through the origin. Live text shows a(n) = a(1) + (n − 1)d with numbers each change.

predictions.evidence: Two real predictions before the reveal: a(10) of 5, 8, 11 as 5 + 10×3 = 35 versus 5 + 9×3 = 32, which exposes the off-by-one before any formula is shown, and where the line of 2, 5, 8 crosses n = 0 (at 2 or at −1, one step before), which sets up the intercept a(1) − d. Each gives a reason for the right and wrong pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five challenge questions each with three options; every wrong option has a why() message naming the slip (off by one step, multiplied a(1) by n, used the first term as c, wrong sign of d, slope and intercept swapped, rounded a non-whole n, term between two terms). The lab also gives instant wrong-answer messages in Build, Points, Formula and Which term? with the box highlighted.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid explanation measures FK −0.9 and adult FK 5.3 with the project readability.fk_grade, well under the 6.5 and 9.5 targets. Sentences are short, terms are named once and then used (common difference, first term, slope, intercept), and numbers are worked in full such as 5 + 9 × 3 = 32 rather than stated.

no_filler.evidence: No filler words (gate_content passed); each kid paragraph does one job: define d and a(1), count n − 1 steps, link to the line and intercept, test if a value is a term. The adult text gives the curriculum codes, the rearrangement and named mistakes. Practice has 4 items and the mastery pool 8, with hints and explanations that show the working.

mobile.evidence: Walked with scripts/pipeline/walk.cjs on iPhone 13 and desktop: every Show me task completes and the challenge finishes. phone_sweep for mt_YgrNBSr2TT reported 0 findings (no overflow, tap targets fine). iPhone dark screenshots show the chart, knobs and n track fitting a 390 px width with buttons beneath; bars and the knobs can be dragged or set with buttons.

accessibility.evidence: axe clean in light and dark themes in the browser gate with no console errors. The canvas has an aria-label and every drag action has a button equivalent (a(1) ±, d ±, Left/Right ▲▼ plus Check, n − 1, n + 1, n + 5), so the lab works without a pointer. Colours use the kit theme A.col, so text and marks keep contrast in both themes.
